results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Bringer of the Last Gift, Superior Spider-Man and Town Greeter.
results.text:
I built a brew: **Sultai "Last Gift" reanimator**.

**The plan:** Superior Spider-Man is the engine. He costs 4 mana (2 generic, blue, black) and can enter as a copy of a creature card in a graveyard. Since you actually cast him, Bringer of the Last Gift's "if you cast it" trigger still works when he enters as a Bringer. That trigger makes every player sacrifice all their other creatures, then returns every creature card that was already in a graveyard. So the deck fills its graveyard early (Town Greeter, Dredger's Insight, Cache Grab and Overlord of the Balemurk each mill four). Then a 4-mana Spider-Man becomes Bringer: it wipes the opponent's board and brings back your Massacre Wurms, Vaultborn Tyrants and Craterhoof. The returning Massacre Wurm gives -2/-2 to anything the opponent gets back, and you lose 2 life for each of their creatures that dies. With Llanowar Elves, this can happen as early as turn 3–4. The target turn is 5.

**How the requested cards fit:**
- **Town Greeter** mills four on turn 2 and grabs a land. If that land is Starting Town (a Town), you also gain 2 life.
- **Superior Spider-Man** is the payoff. If no Bringer has been milled, he can still copy Massacre Wurm (a one-sided sweeper), Vaultborn Tyrant (draws cards) or Overlord, as a 4/4.
- **Bringer** is meant to be milled, not cast for 8. If you draw one, use it as the discard cost for Bitter Triumph. Lotuslight Dancers can also put Bringer straight from the library into the graveyard.

**Directions I considered:**
1. A Sultai self-mill deck borrowing the Golgari Roots mill package: Town Greeter, Dredger's Insight, Cache Grab and Overlord of the Balemurk.
2. A Dimir midrange shell with Spider-Man as a value creature. Town Greeter needs green, so this was out.
3. Golgari Roots plus Insidious Roots, splashing blue for Spider-Man.

I chose the first one because those cards put creatures into the graveyard quickly, and the whole combo depends on that. The mana is based on Golgari Roots, adjusted for three colors.

**Honest caveats:**
- **Odds:** You have Spider-Man by turn 4 about 53% of the time. You see at least one way to get Bringer into the graveyard (mill, discard or Dancers) 98.5% of the time. Each mill-four only has about a 1-in-5 chance of hitting one of the 3 Bringers, so some games you'll copy a Wurm or Tyrant instead.
- **The 0.1% figure:** The submit tool said the full line is drawn by turn 5 in only 0.1% of games. That number assumes you draw every card in the line. Here Bringer, Wurm and Tyrant are supposed to be milled, not drawn, and the tool doesn't count mill or tutors. It doesn't measure how often the combo actually happens.
- **Lands:** It runs 22 lands even though the checker suggested about 25. The 7- and 8-mana creatures are meant to come back from the graveyard, not be cast.
- **The symmetry:** Bringer also gives the opponent back their dead creatures. Massacre Wurm is the answer to that, and Scavenging Ooze is in the sideboard for it.
- **Assassin's Trophy:** It appears in almost no current lists. I kept it because bouncing a creature is pointless when Bringer would just return it, and Trophy also kills Agatha's Soul Cauldron, Elspeth and Overlords.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the meta: Duress against control and Vivi Cauldron, Fell and Feed the Swarm against Izzet Aggro and Dimir Midrange, and Heritage Reclamation and Pick Your Poison against Cauldron and fliers.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Mightform Harmonizer, Spell Snare and Full Bore.
results.text:
I built a Temur (green, blue, red) Landfall brew. It uses the green Landfall deck from the menu as its base and adds a little red for Full Bore and a little blue for Spell Snare.

**The plan:** Cheap creatures that grow when lands enter (Tifa Lockhart, Mossborn Hydra, Sazh's Chocobo, Bristly Bill) come down on turns 1–2, with Llanowar Elves speeding things up. The main kill is Mightform Harmonizer cast for its cheaper warp cost ({2}{G}). Full Bore gives it +3/+2, and since it was warp-cast, also haste and trample. Pump it first, then play the land. Fabled Passage gives two land triggers (the Passage, then the basic it fetches), so (4+3) becomes 14, then 28 trampling, hasty damage on turn 3 or 4. Traveling Chocobo makes every land trigger twice, so even a plain Forest can do it. Spell Snare costs one blue and protects that turn: it counters 2-mana removal like Abrade, Lightning Strike and Bitter Triumph. Early on it can also counter key 2-drops like Vivi Ornitier, Floodpits Drowner and Emberheart Challenger.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Temur Landfall (chosen):** The Landfall package already has the fetch lands, land-doubling (Traveling Chocobo) and creatures that double their power, which Harmonizer needs.
2. **Boros-style aggro with green and blue added:** Real Full Bore lists are 88% Boros Aggro, but that deck has no green, so it can't cast Harmonizer ({2}{G}{G}) or trigger it.
3. **Izzet tempo with green added:** Harmonizer's double-green cost makes it too awkward as a small splash.

I chose direction 1 because it's the only one where all three cards are part of the same turn.

**Honest odds:**
- You'll see at least one land-triggered power payoff by turn 3 about 94% of the time.
- Harmonizer and Full Bore together by turn 5 (on the play) is only about 31%.
- The checker puts the full scripted line, with every card drawn by turn 4, at 0.2%. That number mainly says the exact script is rare, not the deck's real speed: Full Bore and land drops also make Tifa, Hydra or Chocobo hit for lethal-sized damage.

**Mana:** The deck plays 24 lands with 22 green, 12 red and 12 blue sources. Real Landfall lists run about 26 green sources; I gave up a few for the two small splashes, and Elves helps cover that.

**Sideboard:** Mostly aimed at Vivi Cauldron, Izzet and Boros Aggro, and Dimir Midrange:
- 3 Abrade and 2 Burst Lightning
- 3 Surrak, Elusive Hunter
- 2 Repulsive Mutation and 1 Negate
- 2 Seedship Impact and 2 Ghost Vacuum (for Agatha's Soul Cauldron and Reanimator)

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Airbender Ascension, Bramble Familiar and Appa, Steadfast Guardian.
results.text:
I built a Bant (green-white-blue) airbend combo deck around your three cards. It wins with a loop that makes as many tokens as you want.

**The combo:** Doc Aurlock makes spells you cast from exile cost {2} less. Airbending exiles a card and lets you recast it for {2}, so with Doc out every airbended card is free.
1. With Doc and Aang, Swift Savior on the battlefield, flash in Appa at the end of your opponent's turn. Appa airbends Aang.
2. Recast Aang for free. Appa makes a 1/1 Ally token.
3. Aang airbends Appa. Recast Appa for free, and Appa airbends Aang again.
4. Repeat as many times as you like. You get a token every loop, and you untap with a huge army.

Kellan Joins Up turns this into an immediate win. Appa and Aang are both legendary, so every time one enters, every creature you control gets a +1/+1 counter. Doc and your mana creatures can attack the same turn with as many counters as you want.

**What each requested card does:**
- **Appa:** the engine. Every recast from exile makes a token. Without Doc it's still a strong fair card: recasting the deck's 2-drops makes tokens and replays their enter-the-battlefield effects, like Floodpits Drowner stunning creatures.
- **Airbender Ascension:** the backup engine. Enough creatures entering fill it up (the loop does it at once), and then it exiles and returns Appa at every end step. That restarts the airbending even if they kill Aang.
- **Bramble Familiar:** with Llanowar Elves, it gives you eight early mana creatures for a turn-3 Appa or Doc plus Aang. Late in the game, Fetch Quest mills seven and can put Doc, Appa, Ascension or Kellan straight onto the battlefield.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **This one:** the Doc/Aang airbend core from the few winning lists that play these cards, plus the Llanowar Elves ramp package from Simic Ouroboroid and Selesnya Offense.
2. A Selesnya tokens deck using Pawpatch Recruit and Innkeeper's Talent.
3. An Appa deck that just reuses Spyglass Siren and Floodpits Drowner for value.

I chose the first because it's the only one where all three of your cards build toward an actual kill, not just value.

**Odds:** Without mulliganing, you'll have Doc, Appa and Aang together by turn 6 in about 20% of games. The checker counts the full line, including Kellan and Ascension, and that's all in hand by turn 5 in only about 1.9% of games. Most games you'll play it as a fair deck: ramp, use Appa for value, interact with Get Lost and Drowner, and dig for the missing piece with Esper Origins and Aang, at the Crossroads.

**Mana:** I went with 22 lands. The checker suggested about 21 compared with Selesnya Offense, a similar deck with mana creatures. The 15-card sideboard is aimed at Dimir Midrange, Vivi Cauldron and the red aggro decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Abandon Attachments, Firebending Lesson and Combustion Technique.
results.text:
I built **Izzet Lessons Tempo**, a brew. It uses the mana base and Burst Lightning from the proven Izzet Aggro deck (12% of the field), but all three of your Lessons are at the center.

**The plan:** Cheap Lessons do double duty. Firebending Lesson clears blockers for R. Abandon Attachments discards one card to draw two. Each one also puts a Lesson in the graveyard, which turns on the creatures:
- **Fire Nation Cadets** gains firebending 2: each attack adds RR, enough to cast Combustion Technique during combat.
- **First-Time Flyer** becomes a 2/3 flyer.
- **Sokka, Bold Boomeranger** gets a +1/+1 counter every time you cast a Lesson.
- **Dragonfly Swarm** gets bigger: its power equals the noncreature, nonland cards in your graveyard.

By the midgame, Combustion Technique deals 5–6 damage and exiles the creature. Your flyers and burn should finish the game around turns 5–6.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-Red firebending:** the only real list running all three cards. It has removal-heavy Lessons but little that rewards having them in the graveyard.
2. **Izzet Lessons tempo:** borrows Izzet Aggro's mana and burn. Blue adds real Lesson payoffs.
3. **Izzet Lessons control:** Serpent of the Pass, Ran and Shaw and Master Pakku's mill. Too slow against Izzet and Boros aggro.

I chose #2 because blue is where the cards that reward Lessons are.

**Notes:**
- **Lesson odds:** With 12 Lessons plus Sokka's and Tersa's discards to fill the graveyard, you have about an 89% chance to see a Lesson by turn 3 on the play. It's 84% to have both a Lesson and a creature that uses it.
- **Screaming Nemesis is banned.** It's on your list for Izzet Aggro, but the card pool shows it as banned in Standard now, so I left it out.
- **21 lands, not 24:** The deck checker suggested Izzet Aggro's usual 24. I stayed at 21 because nothing costs more than 3 (average mana value 1.77), the mono-red Lesson list played 20, and the kickers on Firebending Lesson and Burst Lightning give extra lands a use.
- **Sideboard:** Aimed at the top decks in your list:
  - Iroh's Demonstration and Obliterating Bolt for creature decks.
  - Abrade and Soul-Guide Lantern for Vivi Cauldron, Reanimator and Artifacts.
  - It'll Quench Ya!, Octopus Form and Ran and Shaw for Dimir and the control decks.

The deck passed the legality check with no warnings.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Ashling, Rekindled, Sunderflock and Bounce Off.
results.text:
I built an Izzet Elementals ramp deck. Every creature in it is an Elemental, so Sunderflock's mass bounce becomes a one-sided board wipe.

**How it works:** Ashling and Flamebraider come down on turns 2–3. Ashling's flip side (Rimebound) adds 2 mana each turn for spells with mana value 4+, and Flamebraider taps for 2 mana that only Elemental spells can use. Together they power out a Deceit or Wistfulness on turn 4. You cast those two with blue mana only, since their hybrid symbols can be paid with blue. Sunderflock costs less by the highest mana value among your Elementals, so with Deceit (6) on the board it costs just 3 mana ({1}{U}{U}) on turn 5. When it enters, it returns every non-Elemental creature to hand, which means only the opponent's.

**Bounce Off's role:** For one blue mana it returns your own Sunderflock to your hand so you can recast it for a second mass bounce. It can also re-use Deceit's or Rimekin Recluse's enter-the-battlefield effects, or clear a blocker. Champion of the Path and Twinflame Travelers are the finishers: with Champion out, Sunderflock entering deals 5 damage to the opponent, and Twinflame doubles that.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Izzet all-Elementals (chosen).** It's the only shell where Sunderflock bounces only the opponent and Ashling's mana always has something to cast.
2. **Simic Ouroboroid.** I'd borrow its Bounce Off/Wistfulness package, but Ashling would need a third color, and Sunderflock would bounce your own non-Elemental creatures.
3. **Grixis reanimator.** This would borrow the Deceit/Overlord package from the few existing Sunderflock decks and add red for Ashling. It has the same self-bounce problem and shakier mana.

**Shell:** The deck checker said most decks with these cards are labeled "Rogue." That label is a catch-all: the latest Rogue list is an unrelated Allies deck, and the actual Sunderflock decks are Sultai reanimator with no red, so I didn't build on them. The mana base copies Izzet Aggro's lands (Riverpyre Verge, Spirebluff Canal) plus 2 Cavern of Souls set to Elemental, so counterspells can't stop your big creatures.

**Odds:** You'll have a 2-mana ramp piece by turn 5 about 82% of the time, a 4+ mana Elemental about 92%, and Sunderflock itself about 57%. Eclipsed Flamekin, Ashling's loot and Wistfulness's draw raise that last number. The checker's 0.6% figure only counts games where you've drawn all six cards in my example sequence, which you never need. The real core is just Sunderflock, one big Elemental and one ramp piece.

**Caveat:** Most of these Elementals (Flamebraider, Champion, Twinflame, Flamekin, Recluse) have no recent tournament results, so this is an untested brew.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the aggro, control and graveyard decks in the current field.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Insatiable Avarice, Doomsday Excruciator and Archenemy's Charm.
results.text:
I built a mono-black control deck around **Doomsday Excruciator**. You stall with cheap removal and discard, cast Excruciator on turn 6, and its enter trigger cuts each player's library down to the bottom six cards. Then **Insatiable Avarice**'s 3-mana mode makes the opponent draw three and lose 3 life, so they run out of cards within about two turns while the 6/6 flier attacks.

**Archenemy's Charm** does three jobs here:
- It's instant-speed removal that exiles.
- It can bring a dead Excruciator back to your hand so you can cast it again. The trigger only works when Excruciator is cast, not reanimated.
- It adds two +1/+1 counters and lifelink to close out a race.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-black control (chosen):** the doomsday plan above.
2. **Dimir Midrange:** borrow the menu's Kaito / Enduring Curiosity package and add Excruciator.
3. **Mono-black demon midrange:** Unholy Annex plus Bloodletter of Aclazotz.

I went with mono-black control, using the tournament mono-black deck's mana (25 black sources) and some of its creatures. Excruciator costs six black mana, which a two-color deck can't reliably cast on turn 6.

**Choices worth knowing about:**
- **Avarice finds the Excruciator.** On turn 5, pay for both modes and target yourself. The search puts Excruciator on top, then you draw three, so you draw it right away. With 4 Excruciator and 4 Avarice, you have about an 85% chance to see at least one of them by turn 6.
- **Bloodletter of Aclazotz** makes the opponent lose double life on your turn. Avarice's 3 becomes 6, and an Excruciator attack becomes 12.
- **Watch your own library.** Excruciator cuts your library to six cards too, and you draw an extra card every upkeep. The opponent normally decks out first: with one Avarice cast on turn 7, their draw on turn 9 is the one that fails. If the game drags on, use Charm to exile your own Excruciator before your upkeep draws run you out.
- **Why there's no Unholy Annex:** I left out the mono-black deck's usual card-draw engine. Its forced extra draw each turn would deck you before the opponent.

**The sideboard** is aimed at the top decks:
- Deathmark, Long Goodbye and an extra Day of Black Sun for Simic Ouroboroid, Landfall and Aang.
- Leyline of the Void and Ghost Vacuum for Reanimator.
- Two more Duress and The End for Jeskai Control and Lessons.

**Honest odds:** The checker puts the chance of drawing every card in the full win line by turn 8 at only 12.4%, but that count includes Bloodletter and ignores Avarice's tutor. The line you'll actually use is just Excruciator plus one Avarice.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Resonating Lute, Inevitable Defeat and Jeskai Revelation.
results.text:
I submitted this as a **4-color brew on a Jeskai Control base**.

**Directions I weighed:**
1. **Jeskai Control with a light black splash (chosen).** This borrows the menu's Jeskai Control package: Lightning Helix, No More Lies, Stock Up, Consult the Star Charts, Get Lost and Day of Judgment.
2. **Lessons shell.** One recent Lessons list did run Resonating Lute. But Lessons is a blue-red deck, and Inevitable Defeat costs {1}{R}{W}{B}, so it would need two extra colors.
3. **Mardu-style control built around Inevitable Defeat**, with Lute added on top. Lute costs {2}{U}{R}, so this ends up four colors anyway, and it would give up Jeskai's tested mana base.

I picked the first one because the latest 5-0 Jeskai Control league list already runs 3 Lute and 3 Jeskai Revelation. That means two of your three cards come with a proven home. Lute's text also solves the third card's problem: your lands tap for two mana of any one color for instants and sorceries, which includes black for Inevitable Defeat. No published list in the last 400 days plays all three together, so this is untested.

**The plan:** Cheap interaction keeps you alive early: Seam Rip, Lightning Helix, No More Lies, Get Lost and Day of Judgment. On turn 4 you land Lute, and from then on your lands make double mana for instants. With five lands that's 10 mana at instant speed. That's enough for Jeskai Revelation (4 damage, two prowess Monk tokens, draw 2, gain 4) plus Inevitable Defeat (exile their best permanent, can't be countered, they lose 3 and you gain 3) in the same turn. Flashback recasts either one from your graveyard. Once your hand reaches seven cards, Lute also taps to draw.

**How the black splash works:**
- The deck has 6 lands that make black: 4 Great Hall of the Biblioplex (makes any color for instants, costs 1 life), 1 Watery Grave and 1 Godless Shrine. Every Lute you draw is another black source.

results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Arclight Phoenix, Buried Alive and Flow State.
results.text:
I built a Grixis (blue-black-red) Arclight Phoenix combo deck. It's a brew: no published list in the last 400 days runs these three cards together. Arclight Phoenix and Buried Alive appear together in just one Modern list.

**The plan:** Buried Alive is a 3-mana sorcery that puts up to three creatures from your library into your graveyard. Here it puts in three Arclight Phoenixes. At the start of combat, each Phoenix returns from the graveyard if you've cast three or more instants and sorceries that turn, and they come back with haste.

- **Main line:** Dark Ritual (instant, turns one black mana into three) → Buried Alive → Flow State. Flow State is a 2-mana sorcery that normally keeps 1 of your top 3 cards. With an instant and a sorcery already in your graveyard it keeps 2 instead, so it refills your hand while counting as the third spell. All three Phoenixes then return and hit for 9 flying damage.
- **Turn-1 kill:** Badlands or Underground Sea → Dark Ritual → Buried Alive → Gut Shot (paid with 2 life) is a 9-damage turn 1.
- **Later turns:** The Phoenixes come back on any turn you cast three cheap spells. Faithless Looting is a second way to get them into the graveyard by discarding them.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Ritual combo (chosen):** Borrows the fast-mana package from the Oops All Spells, Doomsday and Epic Storm lists in your meta summary: Dark Ritual, Lotus Petal and Manamorphose (which pays for itself and draws a card). I picked it because Buried Alive costs 3 mana, and these cards let you cast it and still hit three spells on turns 1–3.
2. **Izzet/Dimir Tempo shell:** Phoenix as a recurring threat behind Daze and Force of Will. Buried Alive does very little in that shell.
3. **Reanimator hybrid:** Buried Alive also finds Griselbrand for Reanimate. That splits the deck between two plans.

**Odds and risks:**
- You see Buried Alive or Faithless Looting by turn 2 on the play about 71% of the time, before counting any card draw.
- Buried Alive plus Dark Ritual or Lotus Petal by turn 2 is about 30%. Brainstorm, Ponder and Flow State are there to raise that.
- The checker gave only 0.8% for drawing every card in the listed line by turn 3. That number is misleading: it requires every named card, including the fourth one (Lava Dart) and the Phoenixes, which Buried Alive tutors for. Assembling it in practice is far more likely than that.
- **Your worst matchups** are graveyard hate (Surgical Extraction) and Consign to Memory, which counters the Phoenixes' return trigger.

**Card choices worth knowing:**
- I kept 1 Gut Shot even though almost no Legacy deck plays it. Paying 2 life makes it a free third spell, and its target (the opponent) is always legal.
- I went to 15 lands. The checker suggested about 14, and Epic Storm lists run about 12.5, but Lava Dart's flashback needs lands to sacrifice. Lava Dart counts toward the three spells twice, once from hand and once from the graveyard.
- The sideboard (Pyroblast, Surgical Extraction, Thoughtseize, Pyrokinesis, Kolaghan's Command, Toxic Deluge, Fatal Push) is aimed at the tempo decks, the combo decks and Tron. Several of those cards are cheap instants that also count toward the three spells.

results.prompt: Brew me a Vintage deck built around Goblin Welder, Legion Extruder and Sewer-veillance Cam.
results.text:
I submitted a Vintage brew built around Goblin Welder, Sewer-veillance Cam and Legion Extruder, labeled as a brew.

**How the deck wins.** The three cards you named make an infinite combo. You need Welder on the battlefield, Cam on the battlefield and Extruder in the graveyard:
1. Tap Welder to sacrifice Cam and return Extruder. Cam leaving the battlefield untaps Welder, and Extruder entering deals 2 damage.
2. Tap Welder again to sacrifice Extruder and return Cam. Cam entering untaps Welder.
3. Repeat. Each loop deals 2 damage, with no limit.

**How it finds the pieces.** Goblin Engineer and Melded Moxite put Extruder (or Cam) straight into the graveyard. The Moxen, Lotus and artifact lands give Welder and Engineer artifacts to sacrifice. The backup kill is Painter's Servant plus Grindstone, which mills the opponent's whole library. Painter set to blue also makes Pyroblast hit any spell or permanent, and turns every card in your hand blue so Force of Will can exile anything.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Chosen: blue-red Welder combo.** This takes the shell from Legacy "Sewer Combo", the only real deck that runs all three of your cards (2 recent Legacy lists). On top of that it adds the Moxen, Force of Will, Ancestral/Time Walk and Urza's Saga package from the Lurrus PO decks in the menu.
2. **Workshop prison** using the Sphere Shops package. Mishra's Workshop can't help cast Welder, and Sphere effects tax your own cheap spells.
3. **Mono-red Ancient Tomb Welder.** Without blue mana you can't cast Cam, which breaks the infinite loop.

I picked the first because it keeps your three cards as the main kill and adds the strongest interaction Vintage has.

**Notes:**
- **Odds:** The draw odds tool gives about a 21% chance of naturally drawing Welder, Cam and Extruder-or-Engineer together by turn 4 on the draw. That figure ignores card draw, the Painter backup kill and mulligans. Ancestral, Brainstorm, Moxite and Engineer's tutor push the real number higher, but this is a combo deck that has to dig for its pieces.
- **Melded Moxite:** The checker flagged it as rarely played in Vintage. I kept it because its discard puts a combo piece into the graveyard, and Vexing Bauble or Gitaxian Probe can't do that.
- **Mana:** 15 lands, close to Lurrus PO's average of about 14.5. Blue sources are 13 against Lurrus PO's 16.6, which is enough because only Cam and a few spells need blue. Red sources are 15.
- **Sideboard:** It targets the menu decks: graveyard hate for Dredge, Mindbreak Trap for the storm-style decks, artifact removal for Shops, and Ensnaring Bridge and Sudden Demise for creature decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum.
results.text:
I built **Boros Metalcraft Soldiers**, a brew on the Boros Synthesizer artifact shell. No published list from the last 400 days plays Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum together, so nobody has tested this combination yet.

**The plan:** Play cheap creatures and cheap artifacts on turns 1–2, so Ardent Recruit gets +2/+2 from having three artifacts out (Recruit's "metalcraft" ability). By turn 3 the Clue from Thraben Inspector, artifact lands and Drum usually do that. Then attack with everything and cast Search Party Captain after combat. It costs {1} less for each creature that attacked, so it often costs just {1}{W} and draws a card. Springleaf Drum has three jobs:
- **Artifact count:** it's a one-mana artifact toward the three Recruit needs.
- **Mana:** creatures you just played can still be tapped for Drum, so it fast-starts a two-spell turn.
- **Repeat value:** it's a cheap artifact for Glint Hawk to return to your hand (instead of sacrificing the Hawk) and for Kor Skyfisher to bounce, then you replay it.

Lightning Bolt and Galvanic Blast (4 damage when you have three artifacts) clear blockers or finish the game around turn 5–6.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-White go-wide**, using the Mono-White Aggro package from the meta list (Inspectors, Battle Screech, Prismatic Strands). It has lots of attackers for Captain, but too few artifacts for Recruit, and Battle Screech's flashback taps the same creatures Drum wants.
2. **Orzhov Glintblade** (Glint Hawk, Cast Down, Lembas). It's a good artifact base, but more controlling and slower than a one-drop Recruit wants.
3. **Boros Synthesizer shell (chosen):** it has the most artifacts (24 counting Clue-makers), Glint Hawk and Kor Skyfisher to reuse Drum, and two burn spells that run on the same three-artifact count as Recruit. Every piece supports the three cards you asked for.

**Notes:**
- I run 18 lands, while real Synthesizer lists average about 20.5. The checker flagged this. I kept 18 because the deck's average mana value is 1.48 (no Lembas or Melded Moxite) and the four Drums also make mana.
- With 4 copies of each named card, you'll see a Recruit or a Drum by turn 3 only about 49% of the time. The plan doesn't depend on them alone: 23 cards make or count as artifacts and 20 creatures can attack for Captain.
- The sideboard targets the current meta: Red Elemental Blast for Terror and Faeries, Dust to Dust for Affinity, Electrickery for Elves and white swarms, Relic of Progenitus for graveyard decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Aurora Eidolon, Sandstorm Eidolon and Spirit Mascot.
results.text:
I built a Boros (red-white) multicolor aggro deck. The idea: the two Eidolons come back from your graveyard whenever you cast a multicolored spell, and every card that leaves your graveyard puts a +1/+1 counter on Spirit Mascot.

**What each requested card does here:**
- **Sandstorm Eidolon:** Pay {R} and sacrifice it, and target creature can't block this turn. That clears the way for your attack.
- **Aurora Eidolon:** Pay {W} and sacrifice it to prevent 3 damage to any target. That saves a creature from burn or a bad block.
- **Getting them back:** After you sacrifice either Eidolon, your next multicolored spell returns it to your hand. The deck has 22 multicolored spells, because red/white hybrid cards count: Boros Recruit, Battlegate Mimic, Fire at Will, plus gold cards like Stonebound Mentor, Skyknight Legionnaire, Pursue the Past and Mascot itself.
- **Spirit Mascot:** It gets a +1/+1 counter whenever one or more cards leave your graveyard. Its 17 triggers are the Eidolons coming back plus flashback spells (Firebolt, Rally the Peasants, Prismatic Strands, Pursue the Past).
- **Stonebound Mentor:** A 3/3 for three that scries 1 off the same graveyard triggers.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Boros multicolor creatures with flashback cards (chosen).**
2. **The Mono-White Aggro / Boros Aggro package** (Battle Screech, Prismatic Strands, Rally the Peasants). It has too few multicolored spells to bring the Eidolons back.
3. **The Mono-Red Rally shell built on Burning-Tree Emissary.** It has almost nothing white to make Aurora Eidolon or Mascot worth playing.

I picked the first because every creature also returns an Eidolon. I did borrow the flashback cards (Rally the Peasants, Prismatic Strands) from the second, and the mana base from the existing Boros Aggro lists. My 19 lands give 15 white and 13 red sources, close to theirs.

**How it wins:** Play cheap first-strikers and Mascot on turns 1–3, and use Bolt and Firebolt to remove blockers. From turn 4, sacrifice Sandstorm Eidolon to stop a blocker, then cast a multicolored creature to get the Eidolon back (and grow Mascot). Battlegate Mimic also becomes a 4/2 first striker for the turn when you do this. Finish with Rally the Peasants (+2/+0 to your team), then flash it back for more damage and another Mascot counter. A typical kill is around turn 6.

**Honest odds:**
- You'll see at least one Eidolon by turn 5 about 72% of the time.
- You'll have a multicolored spell to bring it back almost every game (99.6%).
- The exact six-card example line comes together only about 1.6% of the time. The deck is built so that any Eidolon plus any multicolored spell runs the same loop.
- No published list has played these three cards together, so this is untested.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the current top decks: Red Elemental Blast and Pyroblast for blue decks like Terror, Electrickery for go-wide decks, Dust to Dust for artifact decks, extra Prismatic Strands against the burn-heavy red decks, and Journey to Nowhere and Thraben Charm for big creatures.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Living Death.
results.text:
I built a black-green **Living Death brew**. Living Death acts as your mass reanimation spell and a board wipe at the same time.

**How it wins:** Load your graveyard with huge creatures, then cast Living Death. It sacrifices everything on the battlefield, including all of your opponent's creatures, and then returns every creature card from your graveyard at once. The best line is turn 2 Dark Ritual into Buried Alive, which puts Akroma, Symbiotic Wurm and Visara from your deck into your graveyard. On turn 3 or 4, Living Death (5 mana) comes off a Ritual or Birds of Paradise. Akroma has haste and protection from red and black, so she attacks right away. Visara taps to kill any new blocker. Symbiotic Wurm leaves seven 1/1s behind if it's removed, or if you sacrifice it to a second Living Death. That's about a turn-5 win.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Black reanimator:** Dark Ritual, Putrid Imp and Cabal Therapy with Living Death on top. Fast, but it mostly turns back into the existing Reanimator deck.
2. **Hermit Druid self-mill:** Hermit Druid puts your deck into the graveyard, then Living Death brings it all back. The problem is that Hermit Druid also mills the Living Deaths themselves.
3. **Black-green Survival, rebuilt around Living Death (my pick):** Living Death shows up most in black-green Survival in real Premodern lists. I kept that deck's mana and its Birds/Survival core, then added the reanimator pieces (Dark Ritual, Putrid Imp, Cabal Therapy) and Buried Alive. I picked this because it has the most ways to fill the graveyard (13 cards). Also, Living Death works as a one-sided wrath against the creature decks in the field: Sligh, Goblins, Elves, Madness and Terravore.

**Things to know:**
- **Draw odds:** About 61% of the time you've seen a Living Death (or Insidious Dreams to set one on top) by turn 4. You've seen a graveyard filler 89% of the time.
- **The 0% the checker reported is misleading.** It counts games where you *draw* every card in the line by turn 5, but you never draw Akroma, Visara or the Wurm. Buried Alive and Survival put them in the graveyard. The deck's only white sources are 4 City of Brass/Gemstone Mine, but that's fine because you never cast Akroma or Phantom Nishoba from your hand.
- **Lands:** I ran 20 lands, below the 21–23 the checker suggests. The 7-mana-and-up creatures are never cast, so the deck's real curve is lower than it looks. Birds and Ritual add early mana.
- **Main weakness:** Living Death also returns your opponent's creatures from their graveyard, so watch for that against Hermit Druid or Reanimator. Graveyard removal like Tormod's Crypt is a real threat too, and it's very common in Sligh and Goblins lists. The sideboard includes Withered Wretch, plus Xantid Swarm and an extra Duress against the counterspell decks.
